records.name: Norberts
records.facts_used: Norberts: The name combines Germanic nord, north, and beraht, bright or famous. It preserves an old two-part name structure. The northern element explains a component of the name rather than the birthplace of each bearer. The Latvian Language Agency gives the exact rendering Norbert → Norberts, citing page 63 of a 1960 manual. This dated record illustrates transmission between languages; it is not a first birth registration or proof of one borrowing route in every family.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Siliņš p251 plus exact German given-name rendering; no surname date or bearer-count transfer.

records.name: Laurijs
records.facts_used: Laurijs: Siliņš’s entry points to Laura. This family is based on Latin laurus, laurel. In ancient Rome laurel leaves were used in victors’ wreaths; the symbolism helps explain how a plant word could become established in personal names. Siliņš’s dictionary dates the use of Laurijs: 1932. This records use of the particular name in Latvia. The entry cannot automatically be transferred to similar spellings or treated as the moment the entire name family originated.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Siliņš p209 exact Laurijs under Laura. No independent calendar year supplied.

records.name: Virgilijus
records.facts_used: Virgilijus: The Lithuanian form belongs to Roman Vergilius/Virgilius; Salys explicitly equates Virgilijus with Vergilijus. The clan name’s original meaning is unknown. It cannot be declared a demonstrated derivative of virgo, maiden, or virga, twig. The 1964 calendar reprinted in Salys’s 1983 volume gives Virgilijus (Virgys) on 27 November. This is a concrete printed example of the form’s use. Its position in the historical calendar need not match every modern calendar and is not the name’s invention date.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Salys PDF278 printed263 exact equivalence; PDF317 printed302 November27 has Virgys, not project profile Virgis. DMNES rejects an asserted literal virgo/virga etymology.

records.name: Astrid
records.facts_used: Astrid: The usual Scandinavian explanation is Old Norse Ástríðr from Ás-fríðr, god and beautiful. Onomastician Alhaug also explains the consonant change: after f was lost, a supporting t became established between s and r. Leili Kuusk’s column in the municipal newspaper Leole, November 2005, page 6, uses the exact spelling Astrid. This local explanation documents the name in Estonian print culture. It is neither the name’s first registration nor its year of invention.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: SNL supplies careful Norse derivation; Leole supplies exact dated Estonian use. No Norwegian census or royal popularity effect transferred to Estonia.
